Advanced clustering on real-world data¶

For this practical, you will work in groups (between 2 and 4). You will apply the questions in this notebook to your assigned dataset. (Note that some of the datasets are very large (>10k samples). This might make the execution of some algorithms very slow. If that is the case, do not hesitate to talk to your teacher.)

-

If the submission in eCampus is not working, you can send it to either massinissa.hamidi@univ-evry.fr or kevin.dradjat@univ-evry.fr

We will spend two practical sessions on this notebook: during the first session, you will apply K-Means and Hierarchical clustering. During the second session, you will apply Spectral clustering and compare your obtained results.

Most cells in this notebook are blank, you must fill them in either with code or with written interpretation. Your grade will mostly depend on the quality of your interpretations, make sure to relate your conclusions to the context of your dataset.

Clustering algorithm 1: K-means¶

Apply the K-means algorithm with 2 centers. Look at the default parameters the method takes. Make sure the algorithm doesn't run more than 500 iterations.

What does the max_iter parameter do?

In [21]:
#max_iter is the maximum number of iterations K-Means is allowed to perform in a single run (one initialization/n_init run).
#Each iteration has two steps: assign points to the nearest centroid and update the centroids.
#The algorithm stops early when the change in centroids falls below the tol threshold (or when the labels stop changing);
#otherwise, it stops when max_iter is reached and returns the centroids at that point.

In order to optimize our clusters, we want to apply the silhouette method to obtain the optimal number of centers. Apply silhouette on a range from 2 to 10 centers, display the average silhouette score for each and display the silhouette plot for each center.
For some help, look at the silhouette documentation in scikit learn: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/cluster/plot_kmeans_silhouette_analysis.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-cluster-plot-kmeans-silhouette-analysis-py


Please note that the code below is NOT complete. Fill in the missing parts (they are indicated by ### TO COMPLETE)

In [24]:
range_n_clusters = range(2, 11)

import matplotlib.cm as cm
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_samples


for n_clusters in range_n_clusters:
    # Create a plot
    fig, ax  = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(8,6))

    # This plot is the silhouette plot
    # The silhouette coefficient can range from -1, 1 but in this example all
    # lie within [-0.1, 1]
    ax.set_xlim([-0.1, 1])
    # The (n_clusters+1)*10 is for inserting blank space between silhouette
    # plots of individual clusters, to demarcate them clearly.
    ax.set_ylim([0, len(data[:16000]) + (n_clusters + 1) * 10])

    # Initialize the clusterer with n_clusters.
    clusterer =  KMeans(n_clusters=n_clusters, max_iter=500, random_state=42)
    cluster_labels = clusterer.fit_predict(data_scaled[:16000])

    # The silhouette_score gives the average value for all the samples.
    # This gives a perspective into the density and separation of the formed
    # clusters
    silhouette_avg = silhouette_score(data_scaled[:16000], cluster_labels)
    print("For n_clusters =", n_clusters,
          "The average silhouette_score is :", silhouette_avg)

    # Compute the silhouette scores for each sample
    sample_silhouette_values = silhouette_samples(data_scaled[:16000], cluster_labels)

    y_lower = 10
    for i in range(n_clusters):
        # Aggregate the silhouette scores for samples belonging to
        # cluster i, and sort them
        ith_cluster_silhouette_values = \
            sample_silhouette_values[cluster_labels == i]

        ith_cluster_silhouette_values.sort()

        size_cluster_i = ith_cluster_silhouette_values.shape[0]
        y_upper = y_lower + size_cluster_i

        color = cm.nipy_spectral(float(i) / n_clusters)
        ax.fill_betweenx(np.arange(y_lower, y_upper),
                          0, ith_cluster_silhouette_values,
                          facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, alpha=0.7)

        # Label the silhouette plots with their cluster numbers at the middle
        ax.text(-0.05, y_lower + 0.5 * size_cluster_i, str(i))

        # Compute the new y_lower for next plot
        y_lower = y_upper + 10  # 10 for the 0 samples

    ax.set_title("The silhouette plot for the various clusters.")
    ax.set_xlabel("The silhouette coefficient values")
    ax.set_ylabel("Cluster label")

    # The vertical line for average silhouette score of all the values
    ax.axvline(x=silhouette_avg, color="red", linestyle="--")

    ax.set_yticks([])  # Clear the yaxis labels / ticks
    ax.set_xticks([-0.1, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1])

    plt.title(("Silhouette analysis for KMeans clustering on sample data "
                  "with n_clusters = %d" % n_clusters),
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')

plt.show()

In [ ]:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics.cluster import contingency_matrix
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# Fit KMeans and get labels
kmeans_labels = kmeans.fit_predict(data_scaled)

# Compute the contingency matrix
matrix = contingency_matrix(classes, kmeans_labels)

# Convert to DataFrame for better readability
df_matrix = pd.DataFrame(
    matrix,
    index=[f"True {i}" for i in np.unique(classes)],
    columns=[f"Cluster {i+1}" for i in np.unique(kmeans_labels)]
)

print(df_matrix)

        Cluster 1  Cluster 2  Cluster 3  Cluster 4  Cluster 5
True 0       5312        170       9526       2273        592
True 1      22019         96      21617        971         54

2- Discuss the obtained matrix

The obtained contingency matrix is unbalanced, highlighting the inefficiency of the KMeans method in this scenario. Our dataset contains only one true class, yet the algorithm finds an optimal number of five clusters. Within these clusters, it is impossible to clearly associate them with the true class, as the clusters are highly unbalanced, with some containing very few samples.

We can observe two major clusters and three much smaller, unbalanced clusters, which clearly illustrates the limitations of KMeans in this context. This demonstrates that KMeans may arbitrarily split data even when no meaningful class structure exists, producing clusters that do not correspond to actual classes.

With clustering being an unsupervised learning method, classification evaluation metrics (accuracy, precision, etc) are not appropriate. Instead, we can use clustering evaluation metrics (rand index, adjusted rand index, homogeneity, completeness and V-measure).
Check the scikit learn documentation to understand each score: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#clustering-performance-evaluation
3- Compute all metrics defined above.

In [ ]:

V-measure: 0.052

4- Discuss the obtained scores.

The clustering results are poor. KMeans split a single-class dataset into 5 clusters, producing two main clusters and three very small, unbalanced clusters.

The low scores for Adjusted Rand Index (0.054), Homogeneity (0.066), Completeness (0.042), and V-measure (0.052) show that the clusters do not reflect the true class and are mostly arbitrary.

KMeans is therefore not suitable for this dataset.

If we compare the amount of sample in each cluster for all 3 methods, we can see that the one that would make the most sense is the one with the most balanced amount of samples in each, because we can be more precise with our clustering. Therefore, the best one would be complete linkage, because despite the fact that the cluster are highly not balanced (600 to 60k) it is the one with the smallest difference between the 2 clusters. For some help, look at the silhouette documentation in scikit learn: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/cluster/plot_kmeans_silhouette_analysis.html#sphx-glr-auto-examples-cluster-plot-kmeans-silhouette-analysis-py

range_n_clusters = range(2, 11)   # ### TO COMPLETE: 2 to 10 clusters

import matplotlib.cm as cm
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_samples, silhouette_score
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Standardize the data once
data_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(data)

for n_clusters in range_n_clusters:
    # Create a plot
    fig, ax  = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(8,6))

    # This plot is the silhouette plot
    ax.set_xlim([-0.1, 1])
    ax.set_ylim([0, len(data_scaled) + (n_clusters + 1) * 10])

    # Initialize the clusterer with n_clusters and the linkage method you determined worked best.
    clusterer = linkage(data_scaled, method='complete')  # ### TO COMPLETE
    cluster_labels = fcluster(clusterer, n_clusters, criterion='maxclust')  # ### TO COMPLETE

    # The silhouette_score gives the average value for all the samples.
    silhouette_avg = silhouette_score(data_scaled, cluster_labels)  # ### TO COMPLETE
    print("For n_clusters =", n_clusters,
          "The average silhouette_score is :", silhouette_avg)

    # Compute the silhouette scores for each sample
    sample_silhouette_values = silhouette_samples(data_scaled, cluster_labels)  # ### TO COMPLETE

    y_lower = 10
    for i in range(n_clusters):
        ith_cluster_silhouette_values = sample_silhouette_values[cluster_labels == i]
        ith_cluster_silhouette_values.sort()

        size_cluster_i = ith_cluster_silhouette_values.shape[0]
        y_upper = y_lower + size_cluster_i

        color = cm.nipy_spectral(float(i) / n_clusters)
        ax.fill_betweenx(np.arange(y_lower, y_upper),
                          0, ith_cluster_silhouette_values,
                          facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, alpha=0.7)

        ax.text(-0.05, y_lower + 0.5 * size_cluster_i, str(i))
        y_lower = y_upper + 10

    ax.set_title("The silhouette plot for the various clusters.")
    ax.set_xlabel("The silhouette coefficient values")
    ax.set_ylabel("Cluster label")

    ax.axvline(x=silhouette_avg, color="red", linestyle="--")

    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xticks([-0.1, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1])

    plt.title(("Silhouette analysis for Hierarchical clustering on sample data "
                  "with n_clusters = %d" % n_clusters),
                 fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')

plt.show()

2- Discuss the obtained matrix.

Cluster 1 contains the majority of samples from both classes, especially class 1 (44,638 vs 17,403).

we can still conclude that the last collumn shows that if a sample is part of cluster 1 it's most likely going to be a 1 and if it's part of cluster 2 then most likely to be a 0

The result suggests that complete linkage with 2 clusters is not optimal for this dataset, and alternative linkage methods, more clusters, or different algorithms might achieve better separation.

With clustering being an unsupervised learning method, classification evaluation metrics (accuracy, precision, etc) are not appropriate. Instead, we can use clustering evaluation metrics (rand index, adjusted rand index, homogeneity, completeness and V-measure).
Check the scikit learn documentation to understand each score: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#clustering-performance-evaluation
3- Compute all metrics defined above.

📊 Clustering evaluation metrics:

Rand Index (RI)

Result: 0.5970

Adjusted Rand Index (ARI)

ari = adjusted_rand_score(true_labels, clustered_labels)

Result: 0.0202

Homogeneity

Result: 0.0090

Result: 0.1009

V-Measure

v_measure = v_measure_score(true_labels, clustered_labels)

Result: 0.0165

4- Discuss the obtained scores.

The clustering evaluation metrics indicate that the hierarchical clustering with complete linkage and 2 clusters does not separate the true classes effectively.

The Rand Index (0.5970) suggests moderate agreement with the true labels, but the Adjusted Rand Index (0.0202) shows that, after correcting for chance, the clustering is almost random.

Homogeneity (0.0090) is very low, meaning most clusters contain a mix of different classes rather than pure groups.

Completeness (0.1009) is also low, indicating that samples from the same true class are often split across multiple clusters.

Consequently, the V-Measure (0.0165), which combines homogeneity and completeness, is near zero, confirming poor alignment with the true labels.

Overall, these results demonstrate that the clustering algorithm fails to capture the underlying class structure, likely because the dataset is highly imbalanced and using only 2 clusters is insufficient to reflect the true classes. Alternative linkage methods, more clusters, or different algorithms may yield better separation.

Here is the code i used to answer all the question generate all the answers and dendrogram seen above as well as the matrix, metrics and silhouette.

In [ ]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, fcluster, dendrogram
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import (
    silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score, rand_score,
    homogeneity_score, completeness_score, v_measure_score
)
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

# 1. Load the dataset
print("Loading dataset...")
data_raw = pd.read_csv('smoke_detection_iot.csv', sep=';')
print("Dataset loaded.")
print("Shape:", data_raw.shape)
print("Columns:", data_raw.columns.tolist())

# 2. Keep only numeric columns
data = data_raw.select_dtypes(include=['number']).dropna()
print("Numeric data shape:", data.shape)

# Get true labels (last column)
true_labels = data_raw.iloc[:, -1]

# 3. Standardize the numeric data
scaler = StandardScaler()
data_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(data)

# 4. Do hierarchical clustering with complete linkage
print("Performing hierarchical clustering (Complete linkage)...")
Z = linkage(data_scaled, method='complete')
clustered_labels = fcluster(Z, 2, criterion='maxclust')

# 5. Plot dendrogram
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
plt.title("Dendrogram (Complete linkage)")
plt.xlabel("Clusters merged")
plt.ylabel("Distance")
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode='lastp', p=30, leaf_rotation=90., leaf_font_size=10., show_contracted=True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 6. Silhouette score
sil_score = silhouette_score(data_scaled, clustered_labels)
print("\nSilhouette score for 2 clusters:", sil_score)

# 7. Count samples in each cluster
cluster_counts = pd.Series(clustered_labels).value_counts().sort_index()
total_points = len(clustered_labels)
print("\nCluster counts:")
for cluster_id, count in cluster_counts.items():
    pct = (count / total_points) * 100
    print(f"Cluster {cluster_id}: {count} samples ({pct:.2f}%)")

# 8. Contingency matrix (true labels vs clusters)
contingency = pd.crosstab(true_labels, clustered_labels, rownames=['True'], colnames=['Cluster'])
print("\nContingency matrix:")
print(contingency)

# 9. Compute clustering evaluation metrics
ri = rand_score(true_labels, clustered_labels)
ari = adjusted_rand_score(true_labels, clustered_labels)
homogeneity = homogeneity_score(true_labels, clustered_labels)
completeness = completeness_score(true_labels, clustered_labels)
v_measure = v_measure_score(true_labels, clustered_labels)

print("\nClustering evaluation metrics:")
print("Rand Index (RI):", ri)
print("Adjusted Rand Index (ARI):", ari)
print("Homogeneity:", homogeneity)
print("Completeness:", completeness)
print("V-Measure:", v_measure)

for n_clusters in range_n_clusters:
    # Create a plot
    fig, ax  = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(8,6))

    # This plot is the silhouette plot
    # The silhouette coefficient can range from -1, 1 but in this example all
    # lie within [-0.1, 1]
    ax.set_xlim([-0.1, 1])
    # The (n_clusters+1)*10 is for inserting blank space between silhouette
    # plots of individual clusters, to demarcate them clearly.
    ax.set_ylim([0, len(data[:17000]) + (n_clusters + 1) * 10])

    # Initialize the clusterer with n_clusters. Make sure you use the "affinity"
    # method that gave you the best results.
    clusterer =  SpectralClustering(n_clusters=n_clusters, affinity='nearest_neighbors', random_state=42)
    cluster_labels = clusterer.fit_predict(data_scaled[:17000])

    # The silhouette_score gives the average value for all the samples.
    # This gives a perspective into the density and separation of the formed
    # clusters
    silhouette_avg = silhouette_score(data_scaled[:17000], cluster_labels)
    print("For n_clusters =", n_clusters,
          "The average silhouette_score is :", silhouette_avg)

    sample_silhouette_values = silhouette_samples(data_scaled[:17000], cluster_labels)

    y_lower = 10
    for i in range(n_clusters):
        # Aggregate the silhouette scores for samples belonging to
        # cluster i, and sort them
        ith_cluster_silhouette_values = \
            sample_silhouette_values[cluster_labels == i]

        ith_cluster_silhouette_values.sort()

        size_cluster_i = ith_cluster_silhouette_values.shape[0]

        # Label the silhouette plots with their cluster numbers at the middle
        ax.text(-0.05, y_lower + 0.5 * size_cluster_i, str(i))

        # Compute the new y_lower for next plot
        y_lower = y_upper + 10  # 10 for the 0 samples

    ax.set_title("The silhouette plot for the various clusters.")
    ax.set_xlabel("The silhouette coefficient values")
    ax.set_ylabel("Cluster label")

    # The vertical line for average silhouette score of all the values
    ax.axvline(x=silhouette_avg, color="red", linestyle="--")

    ax.set_yticks([])  # Clear the yaxis labels / ticks
    ax.set_xticks([-0.1, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1])

    plt.title(("Silhouette analysis for Spectral clustering on sample data "
                  "with n_clusters = %d" % n_clusters),

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data = data.drop(columns=["Unnamed: 0"], errors="ignore")
scaler = StandardScaler()
data_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(data)
X = data_scaled[:16000]
y = spectral_labels

# Train a random forest to predict the cluster label from the input features
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X, y)
importances = rf.feature_importances_
indices = np.argsort(importances)[::-1]
feature_importance_df = pd.DataFrame({"Feature": data.columns[indices], "Importance": importances[indices]})

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
plt.title("Feature importance for Spectral Clustering")
plt.barh(feature_importance_df["Feature"][:15][::-1], feature_importance_df["Importance"][:15][::-1])
plt.xlabel("Relative Importance")
plt.ylabel("Feature")

plt.show()

Bonus Question 2: Are the clusters consistent across random seeds?

In [22]:
from sklearn.cluster import SpectralClustering
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score
import numpy as np

seeds = [0, 10, 21, 42, 84]
labels_list = []

# Run Spectral Clustering with different random seeds
for seed in seeds:
    spectral = SpectralClustering(n_clusters=2, affinity='nearest_neighbors', random_state=seed)
    labels = spectral.fit_predict(data_scaled[:16000])
    labels_list.append(labels)

# Compute pairwise ARI between all runs
ari_matrix = np.zeros((len(seeds), len(seeds)))

for i in range(len(seeds)):
    for j in range(len(seeds)):
        ari_matrix[i, j] = adjusted_rand_score(labels_list[i], labels_list[j])

ari_df = pd.DataFrame(ari_matrix, index=[f"Seed {s}" for s in seeds], columns=[f"Seed {s}" for s in seeds])
print(ari_df.round(3))

print("\nAverage ARI between runs:", np.mean(ari_matrix[np.triu_indices(len(seeds), k=1)]).round(3))
# 5-6 min to execute

Seed 42   0.999    1.000    1.000    1.000    1.000
Seed 84   0.999    1.000    1.000    1.000    1.000

In [ ]:
# The ARI score of 1.0 across all runs shows that the clustering results are stable. 
# Different random seeds lead to identical clusters, confirming that the data structure isn't sensitive to initialization.

Conclusion¶

In your opinion, which method gave the better results for this dataset?

In [ ]:
# By comparing the result we can see that spectral clustering is superior to the other methods showing clear link to the class
# The other methods are highly unbalanced and don't show much of a link to the classes (kmeans = 2 big + 3 small clusters / hierarchical = 2 clusters highly unbalanced 600 to 60k)

Usually, when we apply different clustering methods, it's because we do not know the classes. In such situation, we compare the different clustering models we obtained with each method to each other to see if they are corroborating.
Pick two of the three clustering methods used above, and use the same metrics as before to compare them (do not rerun the models, just compare the predicted clusters you obtained with each method).

We chose to compare Spectral Clustering and Hierarchical Clustering because they gave better results on this dataset.

Clustering Comparison: Hierarchical vs Spectral

Hierarchical Clustering

  • Adjusted Rand Index (ARI): 0.020
  • Homogeneity: 0.009
  • Completeness: 0.101
  • V-measure: 0.017

Spectral Clustering

  • Adjusted Rand Index (ARI): 0.418
  • Homogeneity: 0.999
  • Completeness: 0.473
  • V-measure: 0.642

Hierarchical Clustering: Produced clusters that are mostly unbalanced, with very low agreement between clusters and the actual classes.
Spectral Clustering: Produced clusters that are more balanced and coherent, with higher agreement with the true classes, capturing the main class separation more effectively.

Discuss the obtained scores.

Interpretation:

  • Hierarchical Clustering shows very low ARI, homogeneity, and V-measure, meaning clusters do not reflect the true classes.
  • Spectral Clustering performs much better, especially in homogeneity (0.999), meaning each cluster mostly contains samples from the same class.
  • Completeness is moderate (0.473), meaning not all members of a class are captured in a single cluster.
  • Overall, Spectral Clustering provides more meaningful clusters than Hierarchical Clustering for this dataset.

At the beginning of the practical, you noticed the number of classes in the data. After completing all the work, applying silhouette and finding the optimal number of clusters, were you expecting the results you obtained? Can you find an explanation for the result?

In [ ]:
# We were expecting 2 clusters for each method as the class was a binary indicator denoting if the fire alarm went off or not.
# However due to the imperfect factor of the methods and the amount of different features, the result quite different than we expected.
# None of the methods gave exactly 2 clusters as we expected, instead we got 3 or even 5 clusters, which means the features influenced the clustering beyond just the fire alarm status.
